newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn govt aims to cut Bundesbank council, pay - paper.
newsitem.headline: Bonn govt aims to cut Bundesbank council, pay - paper.

text.p: The German government has plans to change the Bundesbank law to reduce the number of council members and employees, cut the length of terms served and reduce pay, German daily Bild newspaper said on Thursday.

Friedrich Merz, a financial expert for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told Bild that after the scheduled introduction of a single European currency in 1999, there would be no need for such a large number of Bundesbank officials.

"If monetary union comes in 1999, we won't need a 17-member central bank council and 16,000 Bundesbank employees any more," Merz told the newspaper. "New council members should therefore no longer be appointed for eight-year terms."

Another CDU member, Heinz Schemken told Bild: "If the Bundesbank law is changed ... salaries should be cut. It is not right that the Bundesbank president should earn more than the Chancellor and that Bundesbank council members should earn more than government ministers in Bonn."
"Central bankers can also be independent when they earn less," Schemken added.

The Bundesbank, which has 17 council members including eight directorate members, itself said in April that it planned to streamline its branch network, cutting down the number of branches to a target of 128 from 167 at the end of 1996.
Members of the central bank's directorate are nominated by the federal cabinet and, after consultation, appointed for a period of normally eight, but certainly not less than two years.
The Handelsblatt business newspaper published a similar report earlier this week but gave no sources for the information.

Juergen Stark, state secretary to the finance ministry, told a briefing on Tuesday that the government had no plans to make any changes to an amendment in the Bundesbank law which is currently going through parliament.
"There are no changes planned to this amendment, which is aimed at bringing the Bundesbank law into line with the requirements of the Maastricht Treaty," he told reporters.
But he avoided commenting on whether a further change in the law could be made at a later date.
